scope.description: Hand-researched deepening pass for the Kamex Mega Battle source slice, emphasizing the July-August 1998 regional tournament circuit, Computer Error participation memory, No.1/No.2/No.3 Trainer placement lanes, and the need to preserve variant tells without overclaiming official copy counts or complete tournament-object coverage.

claims.text: The local catalog, Elite Fourum guide, Pokumon page, and Bulbapedia Computer Error page all place the Kamex Mega Battle regional tournament circuit in July-August 1998.

The local catalog treats Kamex Mega Battle as a child source-slice under the unnumbered pre-English promotional family, preserving four source-pinned rows rather than claiming a complete tournament-object ledger.
The local source slice models four currently source-pinned card identities: Computer Error, No.1 Trainer, No.2 Trainer, and No.3 Trainer.
The Elite Fourum guide frames Kamex Mega Battle as a follow-up to Lizardon Mega Battle and says it was the final tournament series to issue trophy cards with the original No.1-3 Trainer artworks.
Bulbapedia's unnumbered promotional list describes Computer Error as the Kamex Mega Battle participation prize and No.1/No.2/No.3 Trainer as regional first-, second-, and third-place prizes.

The local slice credits Sumiyoshi Kizuki for Computer Error and Mitsuhiro Arita for all three No.1/No.2/No.3 Trainer placement rows. Arita's three-row cluster makes the placement ladder visually continuous; Kizuki's Computer Error makes the participation lane feel like game machinery gone delightfully wrong.

Kamex Mega Battle matters because it is a small tournament apparatus made legible through cards: one broad participation object and three placement objects. The release is not just rare-card glamour; it is the event leaving behind an ordered trail of who played, who placed, and how early organized Pokemon learned to remember itself.

special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent search result names Kamex Mega Battle, Blastoise Mega Battle, Computer Error, No.1 Trainer, No.2 Trainer, or No.3 Trainer.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Preserve the Kamex Mega Battle July-August 1998 route and the participation-vs-placement lane before treating a card as this source-slice row.
steps: Confirm the claimed row is one of the four modeled source-pinned identities: Computer Error, No.1 Trainer, No.2 Trainer, or No.3 Trainer.
Separate Computer Error participation route from No.1/No.2/No.3 Trainer placement routes.
For Computer Error, check Kamex-specific variant tells rather than collapsing it into CoroCoro, Song Best Collection, or English Wizards Promo 16.
For No.1/No.2/No.3 Trainer, preserve the regional Kamex placement lane and do not merge with Lizardon Mega Battle, Challenge Road, or later Trainer trophy rows.
Treat copy counts and venue/winner details as external estimates unless separately evidenced.

narrative.human_title: Kamex Mega Battle: the tournament leaves four fingerprints
narrative.why_it_matters: Kamex Mega Battle is tiny in the catalog and enormous in atmosphere. Four rows carry the shape of a 1998 tournament circuit: Computer Error for being there, No.1 through No.3 Trainer for placing. That ladder is the romance. Early Pokemon was already learning how to turn play into memory, rank into artifact, and a weekend of competition into cards that still feel electric.

claims.text: The local catalog anchors Computer Error (Rocket's Secret Machine), Japanese name パソコン大暴走！, as Kamex Mega Battle source-slice row 045.
The local catalog credits Sumiyoshi Kizuki for the Kamex Mega Battle Computer Error row.
Pokumon describes this Computer Error as a Kamex Mega Battle participation prize and gives an estimated-copy figure; the dossier treats that as a collector estimate, not an official count.

Bulbapedia and Elite Fourum discussion distinguish the Kamex print from CoroCoro and Song Best Collection prints by non-glossy stock and white drop shadow on the Team Rocket R, while glossy CoroCoro/Song Best prints use a red drop shadow.

Computer Error is the democratic half of Kamex Mega Battle memory: not first, second, or third place, but the participation lane. It makes the event's broad floor collectible while its own rules text jokes about a system breaking.

steps: Preserve Kamex Mega Battle participation-prize route.
Check for the Kamex variant tells: non-glossy stock and white drop shadow on the Team Rocket R.
Do not merge with the January 1998 CoroCoro glossy print, Pokemon Song Best Collection CD print, or English Wizards Promo 16.
Treat the 896-copy figure as an estimate unless a separate official source is provided.
Ask for surface/lighting evidence carefully because gloss can be hard to judge from ordinary listing photos.
not_claiming: variant proof from catalog row alone

card_highlights.collector_texture_note: The joke of the card and the seriousness of the event sit right on top of each other.

narrative.human_title: Computer Error 045: the participation lane glitches beautifully
narrative.why_it_matters: Computer Error is funny until you realize how serious its route is. It is the Kamex participation memory: the card you can imagine many competitors carrying home, while the trophy Trainers went to the podium. The white-shadow, non-glossy tell turns a small print detail into a whole provenance question.

claims.text: The local catalog anchors No.1 Trainer as Kamex Mega Battle source-slice row 046.
The local catalog credits Mitsuhiro Arita for No.1 Trainer, matching the three-row Kamex placement-card cluster.
Bulbapedia describes the No.1 Trainer Kamex print as distributed to champions of each regional Kamex Mega Battle conference held between July and August 1998.
No.1 Trainer is the top of the Kamex ladder. It is not merely a rare card; it is first place made portable, the tournament saying this person stood above the field.

card_highlights.collector_texture_note: No.1 Trainer is rank made physical; the number is the event's crown.

narrative.human_title: No.1 Trainer 046: first place becomes an artifact
narrative.why_it_matters: No.1 Trainer is one of the purest forms of Pokemon cardboard as social memory. It is not a monster, not a deck tool, not a booster chase. It is a placement, a person, and a weekend of play compressed into Arita's trophy language.

narrative.human_title: No.2 Trainer 047: the ladder has a middle rung
narrative.why_it_matters: No.2 Trainer is where the podium becomes human. First place gets the crown, third place gets the bronze romance, but second place carries the ache of almost. The card makes that placement durable.

narrative.why_it_matters: No.3 Trainer is the bronze hinge of the Kamex story. It completes the ladder and proves the event cared about more than a single winner. The card is a little ceremony: you were there, you placed, the game remembers.
